notes: SENDIST placement appeal; Wilson J upheld rationality of tribunal findings on dyslexia support at mainstream school.

enrichment.short_title: R v SENDIST: dyslexic pupil's mainstream placement upheld on rationality appeal
key_facts: L, a 14-year-old with dyslexia and high anxiety, attended Vyners School in Hillingdon under a Statement of Special Educational Needs.
Her mother appealed to SENDIST seeking placement at private boarding school Stanbridge Earls rather than the mainstream comprehensive.
After Collins J quashed an earlier tribunal decision, a second panel again found Vyners an appropriate placement.
The mother relied on seven sets of psychometric tests showing attainment well below chronological age; the LEA relied on Mrs Fortune, the SEN coordinator and qualified educational psychologist.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal on a point of law under section 11 of the 1991 Act from a SENDIST decision refusing to amend Part 4 of a statement of special educational needs.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the tribunal's conclusion that Vyners could meet L's needs was not irrational and costs were ordered against the publicly funded appellant with quantification adjourned.
enrichment.ratio: A SENDIST decision on school placement stands unless it is not properly reasoned, not justified by the evidence, or irrational; a tribunal may legitimately prefer the evidence of a specialist teacher who knows the pupil over conflicting psychometric results, especially where anxiety may depress test performance.
legal_issues: Whether the second tribunal was procedurally unfair by having the first tribunal's decision without Collins J's judgment
Whether the tribunal irrationally failed to have regard to psychometric evidence of lack of progress
Whether Mrs Fortune's evidence could rationally outweigh expert psychological testimony
Whether costs should be ordered against a publicly funded appellant

notes: AMP4 procurement preliminary issue; Regulation 32(4) barred Holleran's utilities procurement challenge for delay and lack of promptness.

enrichment.short_title: Holleran v Severn Trent: Regulation 32(4) bars AMP4 procurement challenge
key_facts: Holleran, a contractor with turnover below £32 million, sought to qualify for Severn Trent Water's £1.5–2 billion AMP4 infrastructure programme.
STW used Achilles UVDB and published an OJEU qualification notice in May 2003; Holleran missed the 1 August 2003 joint-venture notification deadline.
Holleran learned of its exclusion on 11 August 2003 but did not issue proceedings until 11 November 2003 after letters on 7 and 10 November.
Holleran alleged inadequate OJEU notice, discriminatory treatment of incumbent contractors and unfair consortium criteria.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Preliminary issue in the Commercial Court on whether Holleran's claim was barred by Regulation 32(4) of the Utilities Contracts Regulations 1996.
enrichment.outcome: Claim declared barred; proceedings were out of time, not brought promptly, and no good reason existed to extend time.
enrichment.ratio: Under Regulation 32(4) each discrete procurement complaint must be brought within three months of when grounds first arose and promptly after pre-litigation notification; ignorance of the law and commercial hope of winning business are not good reasons for extension, and delay inherently prejudices procurement processes.
legal_issues: When grounds for bringing proceedings first arose for each head of complaint
Whether August refusal to extend a consortium deadline created a free-standing breach
Compliance with Regulation 32(4)(a) pre-litigation information requirements
Whether an extension of time should be granted and whether 'promptly' breached Article 6

Jobsin Co UK Plc v Department of Health [2001] EWCA Civ 1241

notes: Food Safety Act section 21(5) case stated; Forbes J granted late leave to include Mr Nicholls and quashed convictions.

enrichment.short_title: Kilhey Court Hotels: due diligence defence restored after section 21(5) slip
key_facts: Kilhey Court Hotel was convicted of ten food safety offences after mouldy food and unclean kitchen equipment were found on 2 April 2002.
The company relied on a comprehensive due diligence system but blamed general manager Mr Bullows and head chef Mr Kenyon, naming them in a section 21(5) notice.
The district judge found Mr Nicholls, head of health and safety, should personally have overseen remedial work after inspecting the kitchen on 25 March 2002.
Because Mr Nicholls was not named in the section 21(5) notice, the due diligence defence failed despite the prosecution conceding it would otherwise succeed.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by way of case stated from Wigan magistrates' convictions, with a late application under section 28A for leave to rely on Mr Nicholls' default as part of the due diligence defence.
enrichment.outcome: Question answered affirmatively that the magistrate was correct on the law as then presented, but leave granted under section 28A, due diligence made out and convictions quashed; appellant ordered to pay appeal costs and magistrates' costs below stood.
enrichment.ratio: Section 21(5) requires notice where the due diligence defence involves another person's act or default; once the tribunal indicates fault by an unnamed employee, leave should be sought to include that person, but section 28A permits the High Court to grant such leave late where justice requires.
legal_issues: Whether failure to name Mr Nicholls in a section 21(5) notice precluded the due diligence defence
Whether the district judge was entitled to attribute partial fault to Mr Nicholls
Power under section 28A to grant leave to amend the due diligence defence on appeal
Appropriate costs orders where conviction was technically correct below but quashed on appeal

R v Bow Street Magistrates Court, ex parte Cow and Gate Nutrition plc (1994) 159 JP 120
Bilon v W H Smith Trading Ltd (2001) 165 JP 701

notes: Planning section 288 challenge; Sullivan J quashed LDC by construing 1961 permission with incorporated site licence application.

enrichment.short_title: Swalecliffe chalet owners: 1961 caravan permission confined to brown land

statutes_considered.title: Caravan Sites and Control of Development Act 1960

key_facts: Seaview Holiday Village at Swalecliffe had long mixed chalet and caravan use; owners sought a lawful development certificate to site caravans on the chalet field under 1961 permission.
The 1961 permission for Kite Farm Camp continued seasonal caravan camp use and incorporated a 1960 site licence application and plan.
The application plan coloured brown land for caravans and yellow land for chalets; chalets did not fall within the statutory definition of caravans.
An inspector granted a certificate permitting caravans on the chalet field; chalet owners challenged under section 288.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application under section 288 of the 1990 Act to quash an inspector's decision granting a lawful development certificate on a section 195 appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Inspector's decision and certificate quashed; planning permission in 1961 extended only to continuation of the existing caravan use on brown land, not yellow chalet land.
enrichment.ratio: Where a 1961 planning permission incorporates a section 17 site licence application and plan, the extent of the existing seasonal caravan camp permitted to continue is defined by that application without extrinsic evidence; chalet land could not form part of the existing site.
legal_issues: Construction of 1961 planning permission with incorporated application documents
Whether section 17 deemed permission covered the whole 29.25 acre site
Extent of the 'existing site' under section 13 of the 1960 Act
Admissibility of extrinsic evidence to cut down express permission terms

notes: Temporary relocation appeal; Court of Appeal held Payne v Payne misapplied to two-year South Africa research posting.

enrichment.short_title: W v A: temporary child removal — Payne v Payne not automatically applicable
key_facts: Unmarried parents of A, nearly four, separated in March 2004 when the mother planned a two-year research posting in South Africa for her PhD.
A lived mainly with the mother five nights a week and with the father two nights; both shared parental responsibility.
The judge refused temporary removal, applied Payne v Payne and made a joint residence order.
Refusal would terminate the mother's university contract and PhD, which required two years' fieldwork in South Africa.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with permission from a family court refusal of leave to remove a child temporarily from the jurisdiction for approximately two years.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; permission to remove granted; joint residence order stood; parents to agree direct and indirect contact arrangements.
enrichment.ratio: Payne v Payne principles governing permanent relocation are not automatically applicable to temporary removal; the more temporary the absence, the less weight those principles carry, and the court must balance career impact against mitigable contact loss over a finite period.
legal_issues: Whether Payne v Payne applied to a temporary two-year removal
Whether the mother's academic career was undervalued as a 'dream' rather than concrete opportunity
Appropriate weight for shared care where the child had a primary home base with the mother
Contact arrangements to preserve the father-daughter relationship during temporary absence
linked_authorities: Payne v Payne [2001] EWCA Civ 166
Re B (Removal from Jurisdiction); Re S (Removal from Jurisdiction) [2003] EWCA Civ 1149

notes: Murder appeal on interview direction; court held jury could not have misunderstood status of interview evidence.

enrichment.short_title: R v Hampson: interview evidence direction did not render conviction unsafe

statutes_considered.title: Criminal Justice and Public Order Act 1994

key_facts: Hampson was convicted of murdering Geraldine Palk in Cardiff in December 1990; DNA later matched his semen to swabs from the victim.
He did not give evidence but in 2001 interviews admitted consensual sexual contact and said she was alive when he left her.
The defence case was that she was killed by someone else after they parted following a casual sexual encounter.
The judge summarised the interviews in detail but did not expressly direct that the whole interview was evidence of truth.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against murder conviction by leave of the full court on ground 5 only: failure to direct that interview answers were evidence when deciding where the truth lay.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; although an express direction should have been given, the jury must have treated the interviews as evidence and the conviction was safe.
enrichment.ratio: Where a defendant's interview contains both incriminating and exculpatory material and he does not give evidence, the judge should direct that the whole statement be considered in deciding where the truth lies; failure to use the standard wording is not unsafe if the summing-up makes clear the interviews are part of the evidence.
legal_issues: Whether the jury were misled as to the evidential status of interview answers
Application of Duncan, Sharp and Aziz to mixed statements
Interaction between section 35 silence direction and reliance on interview account
Whether absence of JSB Direction 55 made the conviction unsafe
linked_authorities: R v Duncan (1981) 73 Cr App R 359
R v Sharp [1988] 1 AC 849
R v Aziz [1996] AC 41
R v Ashton (unreported, 18 June 1999)

notes: Confiscation inadequacy appeal; defendant failed to account for £35,500 and could not obtain section 83 certificate.

enrichment.short_title: Re O'Donoghue: section 83 certificate refused for unaccounted confiscation assets
key_facts: O'Donoghue was convicted in 2001 of obtaining property by deception and theft and received a confiscation order of £94,587.
Realisable assets included a car and caravan sold for less than valued and £35,500 withdrawn from an account in Ms Casey's name.
The Crown Court found he was beneficial owner of the £35,500; about £43,223 remained unsatisfied.
On a section 83 application he sought a certificate for shortfalls on the car and caravan but did not explain what happened to the £35,500.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with permission against Lightman J's refusal of a certificate of inadequacy under section 83(1) of the Criminal Justice Act 1988.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the defendant failed to prove realisable property as a whole was inadequate because he did not account for the £35,500 and possible fruits.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 83(1) the defendant must satisfy the court that his realisable property as a whole is inadequate; where he has possessed an asset he must explain its disposition and cannot obtain a certificate by showing shortfall on some assets while remaining silent on others.
legal_issues: Burden on the defendant to demonstrate current inadequacy of realisable property as a whole
Whether interest or fruits on the £35,500 should be presumed
Relevance of Collins J's decision in Turner
Whether section 83 violates Article 6 by requiring explanation of hidden assets

notes: TCC service dispute over Peacock Centre roof claim; valid service on solicitors and exceptional CPR 6.9 discretion identified.

enrichment.short_title: Peacocks v Taylor Woodrow: valid TCC service and CPR 6.9 discretion
key_facts: Related companies owning the Peacock Centre in Woking claimed extensive roof replacement costs against Taylor Woodrow and Chapman Taylor.
Peacocks issued proceedings just before expiry of a 12-year limitation period and attempted service on Taylor Woodrow's solicitors Campbell Hooper.
Campbell Hooper's April and June 2004 letters related to arbitration and court proceedings; service was attempted on 22 July 2004 but rejected on 3 August.
Parties had cooperated for years under the TCC Pre-Action Protocol and agreed to litigate rather than arbitrate if the notice to concur was withdrawn.
enrichment.procedural_posture: TCC application for declaration of valid service under CPR 6.4(2) and, alternatively, dispensation with service under CPR 6.9 after expiry of the four-month service period.
enrichment.outcome: Declaration that service on Campbell Hooper was valid; alternatively the court would have dispensed with service as an exceptional case under CPR 6.9.
enrichment.ratio: Service on a solicitor is valid where the solicitor has notified the claimant in writing of authority to accept service; objectively construed correspondence inviting all subsequent arbitration-related correspondence to be sent to solicitors can extend to TCC proceedings replacing that arbitration.
legal_issues: Whether Campbell Hooper had authority and had notified Kendall Freeman in writing under CPR 6.4(2)
Whether CPR 6.9 could be used after limitation and service periods expired
Effect of parties' agreement to withdraw arbitration and proceed in the TCC
Fairness of Campbell Hooper failing to warn of defective service before the service period expired

notes: AG Reference for baby-shaking manslaughter; 3-year sentence held lenient but not unduly so; no increase.

enrichment.short_title: AG Reference: three-year manslaughter sentence for shaken baby not increased
key_facts: A 23-year-old father pleaded guilty to manslaughter of his six-week-old daughter Leah by severely shaking her after a sleepless night on 22/23 December 2002.
Leah had feeding difficulties; the offender took her downstairs at about 4 am while the mother slept and she was found moribund at 7.20 am.
Post mortem showed severe head injury consistent with shaking or impact; he denied wrongdoing for about 17 months before pleading shortly before trial.
Morland J sentenced him to three years' imprisonment on 27 May 2004.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Attorney General's reference under section 36 of the 1988 Act alleging a three-year manslaughter sentence was unduly lenient.
enrichment.outcome: Reference dismissed; sentence was lenient but not unduly lenient, and the court declined to interfere having regard to the offender's progress in custody and double jeopardy on reference.
enrichment.ratio: In infant shaking manslaughter cases the range is broadly two to five years; a three-year sentence after a late guilty plea, remorse, isolated loss of temper and good prison progress may be lenient without being unduly lenient, and the court may exercise discretion not to increase on reference.
legal_issues: Whether three years fell below the appropriate range for shaken-baby manslaughter
Weight of late guilty plea, remorse and isolated incident
Effect of 17-month delay in admitting responsibility
Whether double jeopardy and prison progress justify non-interference

notes: GMC judicial review; Elias J refused stay for delay and rejected voluntary erasure before PCC hearing.

enrichment.short_title: Gibson v GMC: delay and voluntary erasure refused in pathology misconduct case

statutes_considered.title: General Medical Council (Fitness to Practise Committees (Amendment) Rules 2002
General Medical Council (Voluntary Erasure and Restoration following Voluntary Erasure) Regulations 2003

key_facts: Dr Gibson, a retired consultant pathologist, faced GMC proceedings for alleged serious professional misconduct in cytology and histology reporting between 1990 and 1995.
Concerns arose from the Kent and Canterbury cervical screening programme and the Wells Inquiry; five patient complaints were referred after screening in 2002.
Dr Gibson sought a stay for delay and voluntary erasure from the Medical Register, which would have stayed the proceedings.
One allegation included possible deliberate misleading of a surgeon reviewing earlier smears.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Urgent judicial review of PCC preliminary decisions refusing a stay for abuse of process/delay and refusing agreement to voluntary erasure before the substantive fitness to practise hearing.
enrichment.outcome: Application refused; a fair hearing remained possible, it was not unfair to continue, the 2002 five-year rule did not apply retrospectively, and public interest required the case to proceed.
enrichment.ratio: GMC disciplinary proceedings are not a special category where mere delay without prejudice requires a stay; Article 6 adds nothing to common law abuse principles here, and voluntary erasure may be refused where serious complaints require public scrutiny despite the doctor's retirement.
legal_issues: Whether delay since 1990–1995 prevented a fair hearing or made continuation an abuse of process
Whether disciplinary proceedings require prejudice before a stay
Retrospective effect of the 2002 five-year misconduct referral rule
Criteria for agreeing voluntary erasure under the 2003 Regulations
linked_authorities: Attorney General's Reference (No 1 of 1990) [1992] 1 QB 630
Attorney General's Reference (No 2 of 2001) [2003] UKHL 68
GMC v Pembrey [2002] Lloyd's Rep Medical 434
